newsitem.title: ZAIRE: US seeks Mobutu-Kabila talks, Zaire rebels advance.
newsitem.headline: US seeks Mobutu-Kabila talks, Zaire rebels advance.

text.p: U.S. envoy Bill Richardson held talks with Zaire's embattled President Mobutu Sese Seko on Tuesday and South Africa said a meeting between Mobutu and rebel leader Laurent Kabila was imminent.

Kabila's rebels said they had entered the provincial town of Kikwit, 400 km (250 miles) from the Zairean capital, after the army fled. Witnesses said by radio from the town that jubilant residents turned out to welcome the rebels.

In Geneva, the U.N. refugee agency said it had received "increasingly shocking reports" of killings of refugees around Kisangani and other areas of eastern Zaire held by rebel troops, and called for a full investigation.
Richardson met Mobutu at his presidential villa inside Kinshasa's heavily defended Camp Tshatshi by the Zaire River and gave him a letter from President Bill Clinton.
"President Mobutu and rebel leader Kabila must meet face-to-face immediately," Richardson told reporters after the 90-minute meeting.
He later left for the southern mining capital of Lubumbashi, Zaire's second city, for talks with Kabila.
"We are after a date. Perhaps we will know more this afternoon. The sooner the better, perhaps this weekend would be an important goal," Richardson said in Kinshasa.
"My meeting with President Mobutu was a good one. We were both very frank. I carried a strong message but at the same time I think we made progress," he added.
South Africa said talks between the two civil war foes, chaired by President Nelson Mandela, were imminent.
"The talks will take place shortly...it will be a meeting between President Mobutu and Laurent Kabila," a spokesman for its Department of Foreign Affairs said in Johannesburg.
He said a venue would be announced in due course.
Mobutu, who has cancer, has ruled out South Africa as too far on health grounds. Kabila has ruled out Congo's capital Brazzaville, over the river from Kinshasa, on security grounds.
Gabon has offered to host the talks. South Africa's Business Day newspaper said a South African naval supply ship could host the talks off Zaire or Angola's neighbouring Cabinda enclave.
A senior rebel commander said in Lubumbashi that Mobutu's Presidential Guard were strongly defending Kikwit airport which rebels need as a springboard for a final assault on Kinshasa.
"We expect to consolidate and have full control of the town later in the day," he said.
Richardson also plans to visit Zaire's rebel-held third city of Kisangani, north of the refugee zone, and possibly Angola, which Zaire has accused of invading to back the rebels.
"We plan to go there (Angola) but obviously the ambassador is flexible about timing," his spokesman Calvin Mitchell said.

Diplomatic sources said there was concern that Angola, struggling to establish its own fragile peace process, could be sucked into the Zaire war with government forces backing the rebels and former UNITA rebels backing the Zairean government.
The rebels, who took up arms in October, now control over half of Zaire, a sprawling nation at the heart of Africa.
Mobutu, who had prostate cancer surgery in Europe in August, posed with Richardson for photographers -- his first public appearance since April 12. He made no comment.
Richardson's trip to Kisangani will focus on the plight of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees and displaced Zaireans.
The rebels have been accused of driving the Hutu refugees into the jungle in the hope that they will die there. Kabila has given aid agencies 60 days to repatriate them.

"We are receiving increasingly shocking reports of killings of refugees both in the area around Kisangani and elsewhere," Pamela O'Toole, spokeswoman of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), said in Geneva. "These killings must stop and an urgent investigation must be launched."
